quiz.title: Chapter 10 Quiz: Legislative History
quiz.intro: Ten questions on when to open the legislative record, what each document is worth, and how to find it.

items.q: According to the chapter, when is opening the legislative record justified?
options: Only when the statute is ambiguous as to a term and no higher-authority source (text, case law, regulations) resolves it
At the start of every project
items.why: Legislative history is persuasive and many courts discount it, so consulting it before establishing ambiguity is wasted effort (Legislative History and the Research Cycle).

items.q: Which documents carry the most interpretive weight?
items.why: Conference reports represent both chambers’ final agreement on disputed language (The Most Important Sources and Their Weight).

items.q: A floor statement’s weight depends in part on:
options: The time of day it was given
Whether the speaker was a sponsor or floor manager, and whether it was actually spoken rather than inserted into the Record
items.why: Members may insert statements never spoken on the floor; those carry reduced weight (How Legislative History Is Made).

items.q: If “knowingly” was added to a criminal statute late in the process, bill versions suggest:
options: An intent to require proof of mental state
Nothing; bill versions carry no weight
items.why: Bill versions and amendments are moderate-weight evidence of how language evolved (The Most Important Sources and Their Weight).

items.q: The first step in searching for a federal law’s legislative history is:
options: Searching the Congressional Record by keyword
Starting from the statute’s credit line in the annotated code: the Public Law number, Statutes at Large citation, and year
items.why: For the ADA that is Pub. L. No. 101-336, 104 Stat. 327 (1990); then find the bill number and Congress (Searching for Legislative History).

items.q: Before building a legislative history yourself, the chapter says to:
options: Check whether a compiled legislative history already exists
items.why: Compiled histories can save enormous time on significant public laws (Searching for Legislative History).

items.q: Which free source provides official GPO PDFs of committee reports, hearings, bill versions, and the Congressional Record?
items.why: Congress.gov is also free and comprehensive for modern legislation (Searching for Legislative History).

items.q: The textualism debate matters to a researcher because:
options: Whether the court that will hear your case is textualist or purposivist determines how much of this chapter’s machinery to deploy at all
It decides which committee reports exist
It is tested on the bar exam
items.why: That is itself a research question worth answering early (The Textualism Debate).

items.q: An agency’s interpretation of a statute belongs to:
options: Administrative history, not the record of what the legislature intended
items.why: Confusing the two is a pitfall the chapter names (Common Pitfalls).

items.q: Why does the chapter say state legislative history is often unavailable, and what follows from that?
options: States hide their records; file suit
Many states preserve little, so their courts rely more on text and canons; recognizing that keeps you from hunting for documents that were never created
All states have archives like California’s
You should use federal history instead
items.why: That is not a research failure; it is a reality of state documentation practices (State Legislative History Research).
